\(P([[if test="is(ix=1)"]]3^\circ\,15'\,\mathrm{N}, 38^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=2)"]]2^\circ\,50'\,\mathrm{S}, 41^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=3)"]]6^\circ\,20'\,\mathrm{S}, 42^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=4)"]]1^\circ\,35'\,\mathrm{N}, 36^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=5)"]]12^\circ\,10'\,\mathrm{N}, 55^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=6)"]]7^\circ\,55'\,\mathrm{S}, 40^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=7)"]]18^\circ\,30'\,\mathrm{S}, 57^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=8)"]]0^\circ\,40'\,\mathrm{N}, 44^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=9)"]]5^\circ\,05'\,\mathrm{N}, 48^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=10)"]]9^\circ\,45'\,\mathrm{S}, 39^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]])\) and \(Q([[if test="is(ix=1)"]]11^\circ\,40'\,\mathrm{N}, 38^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=2)"]]9^\circ\,25'\,\mathrm{N}, 41^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=3)"]]14^\circ\,05'\,\mathrm{S}, 42^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=4)"]]4^\circ\,50'\,\mathrm{S}, 36^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=5)"]]25^\circ\,45'\,\mathrm{N}, 55^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=6)"]]3^\circ\,20'\,\mathrm{N}, 40^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=7)"]]4^\circ\,45'\,\mathrm{S}, 57^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=8)"]]13^\circ\,25'\,\mathrm{S}, 44^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=9)"]]21^\circ\,50'\,\mathrm{N}, 48^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]][[if test="is(ix=10)"]]2^\circ\,10'\,\mathrm{N}, 39^\circ\,\mathrm{E}[[/if]])\) are on the meridian \({@lon@}^\circ\,\mathrm{E}\). Take \(\pi = \tfrac{22}{7}\) and \(R = 6370\,\text{km}\). Distances in km within 0.1% of the exact value are accepted.

(a) Find the distance \(PQ\) along the meridian in nautical miles.

[[input:ans1]] nm [[validation:ans1]] [[feedback:prt1]]

(b) Find \(PQ\) in kilometres, to the nearest km.

[[input:ans2]] km [[validation:ans2]] [[feedback:prt2]]

generalfeedback.text:
(a) [[if test="same"]]\(P\) and \(Q\) are on the same side of the equator, so subtract the latitudes.[[else]]\(P\) and \(Q\) are on opposite sides of the equator, so add the latitudes.[[/if]] [[if test="same"]]\({@floor((hi)/60)@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(mod(hi,60)<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@mod(hi,60)@}' - {@floor((lo)/60)@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(mod(lo,60)<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@mod(lo,60)@}' = {@floor((nm)/60)@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(mod(nm,60)<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@mod(nm,60)@}'\)[[else]]\({@floor((a)/60)@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(mod(a,60)<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@mod(a,60)@}' + {@floor((b)/60)@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(mod(b,60)<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@mod(b,60)@}' = {@floor((nm)/60)@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(mod(nm,60)<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@mod(nm,60)@}'\)[[/if]]. A meridian is half of a great circle, and a nautical mile is one minute of arc on a great circle, so the difference in minutes is the distance in nautical miles: \({@D@} \times 60 + {@M@} = {@nm@}\), so \(PQ = {@nm@}\) nm.

(b) The angle at the centre is \({@nm@}' = {@dispdp(float(nm/60),3)@}^\circ\), so

\[PQ = \frac{ {@dispdp(float(nm/60),3)@} }{360} \times 2 \times \frac{22}{7} \times 6370 = {@dispdp(float(kmv),1)@} \approx {@floor(kmv+1/2)@}\,\text{km}.\]

Or use \(1\) nm \(= 1.853\,\text{km}\): \({@nm@} \times 1.853 = {@dispdp(float(nm*1.853),1)@}\,\text{km}\).

questiondescription.text:
Navigation: distance along a meridian

Grade 12 CBE Core 2.7 (c) / Essential 2.3 (d): Find the distance between two places on the same meridian in nautical miles and in kilometres.

Core and Essential

This question is adapted from Chapter 3 (The sphere), Exercise D, question 8 of School Mathematics Project, SMP Book 5 (Metric), ed. P. G. Bowie, Cambridge University Press, 1969: great-circle distance along a meridian; kilometres added, new positions.

INNODEMS CBC Grade 12 Mathematics, first draft by Ben Davies, 2026. Aligned to the KICD Senior School Curriculum Design, Core and Essential Mathematics Grade 12 (draft).

truefeedback.text: [[if test="same"]]\(P\) and \(Q\) are on the same side of the equator, so subtract the latitudes.[[else]]\(P\) and \(Q\) are on opposite sides of the equator, so add the latitudes.[[/if]]

You read \({@D@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(M<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@M@}'\) as the decimal \({@D@}.[[if test="is(M<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@M@}\). There are 60 minutes in a degree, not 100: change the degrees to minutes and add the \({@M@}\) minutes.
That is the difference in degrees. A nautical mile is one minute of arc, so give the difference in minutes.

falsefeedback.text: Your \({@ans1@}\) nm is \({@ans1@}'\) of arc on the meridian, which is \({@dispdp(float(ans1/60),2)@}^\circ\). Compare that with the difference in latitude between \(P\) and \(Q\), worked in degrees and minutes.

truefeedback.text: You used \(\pi R\) instead of \(2\pi R\) for the whole circle.
You read \({@D@}^\circ\,[[if test="is(M<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@M@}'\) as the decimal \({@D@}.[[if test="is(M<10)"]]0[[/if]]{@M@}^\circ\). The \({@M@}\) minutes are sixtieths of a degree, not hundredths.
[[if test="same"]]\(P\) and \(Q\) are on the same side of the equator, so subtract the latitudes.[[else]]\(P\) and \(Q\) are on opposite sides of the equator, so add the latitudes.[[/if]]
Your conversion is right for your answer to (a), but (a) is wrong.

falsefeedback.text: [[if test="yshow"]]Your answers to (a) and (b) make one nautical mile equal to \({@dispdp(yr,3)@}\,\text{km}\). [[/if]]One nautical mile is \(1.853\,\text{km}\). You can also work from the angle at the centre, as a fraction of the whole circle.
